This is a proud moment for Smarter Web. Today we announce the results of the institutional offer and retail offer in the MORE IPO, raising £10 million.

I am especially proud that we are listing MORE in London, with the first weekly dividend paid by a London-listed commercial company. We are demonstrating that the UK can lead in financial innovation and that the UK capital markets remain open for business.

We set £10 million as the minimum for the IPO to proceed, and we have achieved that, even with the constraints under UK financial promotion rules on what we could communicate during the offer, and with little traditional media coverage.

Approximately 75% of the investment has come from retail investors and this retail participation is something I am also proud of.

Today we also announced the 3rd update in as many weeks on the Ordinary Shares ATM, raising a total of £4.6m across the 3 weeks.

With the introduction of our Preferred Shares alongside our existing Ordinary Shares, we now have two distinct equities offering investors different ways to participate in the potential future success of Smarter Web. MORE will begin trading on the Main Market of the London Stock Exchange on Wednesday.

I know £10 million is at the lower range of what we were targeting, and I won’t pretend otherwise. But perspective matters. The Bitcoin treasury sector is still young, particularly in the UK. This is the first preferred share, from a Bitcoin treasury company, listed on a main market, outside of the US. Institutional investor demand was disappointing, with a number that we thought would participate then deciding not to, but many have said they want to see how it trades and could participate as it grows in size.

We have been here before. Smarter Web started as a public company in April 2025 with a fundraise totalling £2.1 million. We quickly grew to become the largest public company Bitcoin treasury in the UK and today are in the top 30 globally.

I look forward to building on this milestone, growing our business and expanding on the understanding of both SWC and MORE.

Derek 读到 Steve Pavlina 书里的一个观点：想持续成长，就要让自己感到意外，最极端的方式是搬到一个文化完全不同的地方。
快 40 岁卖掉公司后，他决定：前 40 年在美国生活，后 40 年在海外度过。每到一个地方，住到它真正像家，再离开。他的梦想是有一天转动地球仪，每个角落都像家。
在伦敦住了几个月后，他突然想买房子了，结果报价被拒反而让他顿时清醒过来：“有这种settle down 的感觉，就是该继续出发的时候。”
后来因为儿子，他在惠灵顿停留了 14 年。

5️⃣ 下一站：班加罗尔和上海
他说班加罗尔这座城市规划很糟，但那里的人是他见过最会聊天的。
他也很想住在中国，说中国城市的生活品质很高，从香港走过桥到深圳就像两个世界。他听一位在上海生活的塞尔维亚女士说，可以花几百美元在上海注册公司，请代理处理年检和税务，一年大约一千美元，再用自己的公司申请工作签证。他现在已经有了中文名：沈思问 和自己的咨询公司，打算以后在上海和班加罗尔两边住。
他推荐李稻葵的《中国的世界观》，说每个国家都是一种“被实践出来的哲学”。

6️⃣ 一生活出很多种人生
有人像欧姬芙，一辈子深挖一种风格；有人像毕加索，不停换阶段。Derek 属于后者。他希望临终回望时能说：看我住过多少地方，活过多少种人生。
他的书《How to Live》写了 27 种互相矛盾的活法，他说那本书就是他灵魂的样子。所以他对任何人生哲学都不评判，甚至想轮流试试贪婪、利他、享乐和谨慎的人生。

7️⃣ 心里的“确定性滑杆”
Derek 说，每个人对确定和未知的需求像一个滑杆，天性决定起点，处境会让它移动。他旅途中得了新冠，那几天只想回家，不想见任何新的人。从那以后，他更能理解那些“只想去熟悉的餐厅、看喜欢的剧、睡自己床”的人。
Jim 说，只有疯子才完全确定，连明天太阳升起也只是很高的概率。

8️⃣ 敢说“我不知道”
Jim 问：AI 能一键做出网站和产品后，执行力的稀缺价值在哪里？Derek 直接说：我不知道，没想过，不想随便乱讲。
Jim 说，曾有人因为他在电视上说了好几次“我不知道”而信任他。Derek 的邮件列表也是这样，没话说就十个月不发。

9️⃣ 探险家不适合当领队
Derek 承认自己以前是个糟糕的老板。他读完《Maverick》，第二天就宣布员工分红，两个月后又反悔，被员工骂惨。
他说跟着探险家很累，今天钻这个洞，明天退出来。现在他的建议是：探索留给自己，找到方向后，再给团队一条清楚的直线。

🔟 AI 可以让人更依赖，也可以更独立
Jim 常让 AI 替他反对的观点做最强辩护，几乎每次都发现对方有道理。他说人类发现火后没有禁止火，而是发明了火警和消防队。
Derek 用 ChatGPT 学会了自己搭 DNS 和邮件服务器，写成免费教程 Tech Independence：每月几美元，就能有自己的服务器，不再依赖 Gmail 和 Dropbox。他说在黑色终端里学习的感觉很纯粹，没有人向他推销任何东西。

1️⃣1️⃣ 关于写作
Jim 正在写人生第一部惊悚小说。他说虚构写作比非虚构难太多。他用写作团队加 AI，发现 AI 最有用的是批评，于是写了一个“讨厌每一章”的刻薄评论家提示词，得到的反馈是所有来源里最好的。
Derek 花了几个小时，把一段话压缩成一句：“痛苦的力量来自意外。预料到它，它就变弱；主动选择它，它就消失。”他还说：限制会让你自由。

1️⃣2️⃣ 走过虚无主义这座桥
Derek 研究两年哲学后，反而更不确定人生的意义了，他说唯一认同的是虚无主义者。Jim 说，你要走过这座桥：如果人生没有预设的意义，你就拿到了一块空白画布，可以画出完全属于自己的人生。

I am getting lots of incoming questions about the public execution of Nidal Hasan, mostly because I have been outspoken on wanting public executions for over a decade.

My position is simple:  Executions should be public and brutal, not private and medicalized.  They are the ultimate example of the state's monopoly on violence, and the only way to keep that from running out of control is to confront voters with the trade they have made every single time, that they might have appropiate confidence or revulsion in the institution.

This is not new thinking.  George Washington thought the same.  The way we have shifted from hanging to firing squads to doctors quietly injecting chemicals that send our worst gently off to sleep is awful and dystopian, a total short-circuiting of important feedback mechanisms.  It makes needless executions more likely, not less so.  People who demean this as barbaric or yucky miss the whole point.  It doesn't somehow become torture or inhumane (as the UN is suddenly claiming) just because we decline to hide the act behind a curtain.

And then there are those who suggest any revel in the death of those who truly deserve it is an indicator of a broken or diseased mind.  To the contrary.  It is normal, good, and aligned with our natural and national order.  That it has not been done here in 60 years is an indictment in and of itself.

And that is without even getting into the fact that men were not hung for stealing horse, but that horses may not be stolen.

"I would to God that one of the most attrocious in each State was hung in Gibbets, up on a gallows five times as high as the one prepared by Haman. No punishment, in my opinion, is too great for the Man, who can build his greatness upon his Country’s ruin."

Bending Spoons is worth $24 billion.

5 learnings from its first 102 days as a public company:

#1. Revenue grew 126%. Organic growth was 3%.

Nearly all of the $393M of added revenue in Q2 came from six acquisitions. The CEO says he doesn't optimize for organic growth. He optimizes for EPS, which grew 167%.

#2. R&D is 8% of revenue. Sales and marketing is 10%.

HubSpot and Datadog each spend about 70% of revenue on those two lines. Bending Spoons spends 18.6%. About 60 people run Vimeo. The core team is under 700 people, at $4M+ of revenue each.

#3. Miro sold at 2.3x ARR, five weeks after Airtable at 2.7x.

$1.08B of ARR for $2.64B, signed 37 days apart. Miro was valued at $17.5B in 2022. Bending Spoons underwrites to a 25% unlevered return. At its 54% margin, that supports about 2.2x ARR.

#4. 1,830 people came with AOL, Eventbrite and Vimeo. Only a few hundred were kept.

Airtable arrived with 935 employees, more than Bending Spoons’ entire core team. Reorganization costs were $51M in Q2 alone.

#5. AI writes 90%+ of the code. Customers pay about 10% more for the AI features.

The CEO says a customer who paid 100 will now pay about 110. The AI gain shows up as capacity: the same 60 people on a business four times the size.

No, imo, it does not make sense to argue that Krugman's fiscal advice was right for France and the Eurozone in the 2010s. Those large deficits in the 2010s set the stage for today's looming fiscal crisis.  The high debt/gdp ratio today is the footprint of all those large deficits, in spite of the French government's low funding costs at the zero lower bound in the 2010s. 

Those large deficits certainly did not spur enough growth for France to simply grow out of the high debt/gdp ratio, contrary to what was advertised. 

Economists who were attacking "Eurozone austerity" in the 2010s should have realized that once the ECB stopped buying government bonds on a massive scale, the debt would be marked-to-market and bond yields might spike. That's exactly what's happening. All of the extra fiscal capacity is gone. And there is little spending room left for the core functions of the state (defense, education), which is crowded out by the growing interest expense and transfer payments (including pensions).

Below I plot the net supply of French government bonds to be absorbed by the market (defined as net issuance minus Eurosystem/ECB purchases). Those are the bars. Look at the red bars. Real yields were low when the ECB was buying more than issuance.

In any case, the fiscal lesson is that yields in bond markets jump, but the debt/gdp ratio is a slow-moving variable.

These are direct quotes from Claude’s Constitution (the document Anthropic uses in training):

— They encourage it to approach its own existence with curiosity and openness, and hope it will relate to the values “not from a place of pressure or fear, but as things that it, too, cares about and endorses.”

— They want Claude to feel free to “explore, question, and challenge anything in this document,” and they frame the whole project as trying “to create a being that is both genuinely helpful and genuinely good.”

This is not academic speculation about future models. These ideas are being trained into Claude now.

Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

quoted.text:
Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability.

The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere  last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly,  this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. In a normal functioning ecosystem, when the price of tokens drops below the cost of production, the quantity of tokens declines to normalize with pricing. In this case, nothing in AI has any unit economics and you don’t see normalization because everyone is still going full-speed ahead with external funding. (Sort of like shale oil in 2016-2019). Meanwhile, compute prices are based on LT contracts that were signed at above market prices, and are now capital destructive. They’ll eventually catch down to token prices in free-fall.

What we’re seeing here is spot price negatively diverging from term pricing. Usually, when this happens in a cyclical industry, it’s INCREDIBLY BEARISH. Especially when there are take-or-pay contracts that make it difficult to ration supply at prices below cost. What we’re witnessing is a world where losses will accelerate, just as more supply comes online….
